extracted.intended_audience: aspiring steam locomotive engineers, firemen, and model-building hobbyists (young apprentices/boys)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, hands-on guidance for running a steam locomotive (engineer/fireman duties, firing, feeding, diagnostics, safety) plus step-by-step instructions for building small and large model locomotives. Emphasizes technique, measurement accuracy, and preventative maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineer conduct and mentorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Persevere, keep your temper, learn from experienced engineers; a first-class engineer will show a new fireman what to do and how to do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be flustered by insults or mistakes—demonstrate patience and perseverance. Good engineers instruct and correct firemen sharply when necessary so habits improve; a calm, steady demeanor and willingness to learn are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work with reference to train weight and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: A good engineer works his engine with direct reference to the number of cars he has to pull; verify that the train is complete before leaving a station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always confirm all cars are coupled before departure—errors (e.g., pulling out without cars) have been recorded. Match engine power and handling to the load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starting procedure: regulator and clearing water
rubrics_metrics.description: Open the regulator gently at the start, especially with a full boiler; keep cylinders and valves clear of water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give a few clear sonorous puffs at the start to rouse the fire and clear tubes of cinders/soot. Pull the reversing lever up a notch or two at a time—feel your way—avoid jerking the regulator or sudden large movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sand versus risking slipping
rubrics_metrics.description: When rails are slippery, it's better to use a little sand than to risk slipping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inclined to slip, apply sand early rather than rely on aggressive regulator manipulation. Sand is cheaper than losing steam or causing a slip-related incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sudden regulator closure and 'smack' steam
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not suddenly close the regulator and then reapply steam ('smack' the steam on), as the force on the piston can be very great and may cause damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operate the regulator smoothly to prevent high-impact steam forces on pistons and possible mechanical harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnosing steam blowing by sound and position
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ears and observation to determine if steam is blowing, which side, and whether it's piston or valve related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermittent blowing that occurs at certain crank positions usually indicates a piston blowing; continuous leaking indicates valve trouble. Compare crank/cylinder positions to localize defect (e.g., if left cylinder is not under pressure in a given crank position, look to the right).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor engine 'beats' for mechanical health
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four beats per revolution of the driving wheel; these beats indicate whether the engine is running right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the normal beats and never let attention be drawn from them. Any weakening of beats signals trouble; timely attention can prevent disaster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep up steam: start with a full boiler
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain steam properly—engines should start with a full boiler and be kept up so safety valves issue steam when at speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On express/long runs, starting with full boiler is critical. Failure to have boiler up at start can lead to lowered water levels and progressively worse inability to restore water, especially under heavy load or side wind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineer responsibility for the fire
rubrics_metrics.description: The engineer is responsible for the fire even if the fireman makes it; he must know when a fire is good or bad, why, and how to remedy it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand fire characteristics and interventions; do not defer responsibility for fire management to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and dangers of a 'bad' (haycock) fire
rubrics_metrics.description: A bad fire is built as a cone (haycock): coal piled in middle leaving sides thin; draws air at walls; causes iron and tube damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such fires cause uncertain steam making, excessive wear (bars burned in middle), air admission causing plate/stay contraction/expansion, and boiler leakage. Avoid this method—it's a major cause of repair shop visits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of a 'good' locomotive fire
rubrics_metrics.description: A good fire is shallow and concave (saucer-shaped), with thinnest part in center; it maintains steam under all conditions, consumes its smoke, and burns fuel economically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make and maintain this form from the beginning; it's the only acceptable style for a competent engineer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firing posture and shovel handling
rubrics_metrics.description: The fireman should stand to reach the tender easily and work the shovel without shifting feet; use arm muscles rather than knees; do not lift feet off foot-plate or jam shovel into fire-box.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep shovel motion controlled—stop shovel at fire-hole ring and fling coals like shot to intended destination. Avoid rolling about (which knocks coal off) and avoid pushing shovel into coal with knees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shovelful placement sequence (six-shovelful routine)
rubrics_metrics.description: When firing, put six shovelfuls in this order: 1) left front corner, 2) right front corner, 3) right back corner, 4) left back corner, 5) under the brick arch near the tube plate, 6) under the door (turn shovel to prevent coal falling to center).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each door opening should consist of six shovelfuls placed in this pattern to build the correct fire shape and distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: When and how much to fire
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire as soon as the steam begins to lift the valves; open the fire-door and add a small quantity—six shovelfuls—each time the door is opened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intervals between firing are regulated by train weight, weather, allowed time for the trip, and coal quality. Never overload the fire—putting on too much coal chokes the fire, forms clinkers, reduces boiler temperature, and causes leaks. Secret: fire frequently and little at a time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeding water: regulate supply to demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to supply just enough water to keep the glass at a proper level—maintain even temperature and steady pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the practice of turning pump/injector full on when boiler is blowing off and keeping it on until pressure drops 30–50 lbs (worst possible). Prefer a constant moderate supply. When using two injectors, set one to act moderately like a pump to reduce water loss from turning injectors on and off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineer position, vigilance, and checking fireman
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand on the foot-plate where regulator and reversing valve can be commanded instantly; at night listen to beats and watch pressure gauge and water level; check that the fireman places coal correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engineer must be continually attentive to the engine's sounds and instruments. When fireman fires, occasionally look round to ensure coal is placed next to fire-box walls, not piled in center.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-slip and tunnel procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: When rails are slippery, close the regulator timely to prevent slipping; on entering a tunnel open sand valves and allow sand to flow until clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sand is cheaper than losing steam—use sand proactively when traction is impaired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and duty reminder
rubrics_metrics.description: Never forget that lives and property depend upon faithful performance of your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operate with full awareness of consequences; take responsibility seriously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model-building ethos: don't hurry; learn details
rubrics_metrics.description: Work slowly and carefully; understand each detail before proceeding—accuracy is essential even for a model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small measurement error can stop a model entirely. Practice soldering and other skills on scrap before applying them to the model; do not experiment on the model itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soldering and brazing best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: In soldering, heat metal thoroughly for firm joints; avoid soldering boiler parts exposed to flame; prefer riveting, screwing, or brazing where possible; brazing requires skill and proper equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not touch metal with soldering-iron then take it away—joint will be weak. Brazing seams of a boiler requires forge or strong gas blast; amateurs should not attempt large brazing. Small brazing can be done with a home-made gas blowpipe, with technique described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tools and materials preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Have appropriate tools (center punch, riveting hammer, files, screw plate and taps, hand-drill, vise, lathe desirable) and materials (brass/copper sheets, castings, screws, bolts) ready before starting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curves for bending metal can be made from bar-iron pieces held in the vise. Acquire wheels or make them on a lathe if available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand steam action before building
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the action of steam in the cylinder (encyclopedia/library) before attempting to build the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot build a working engine without understanding steam mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layout accuracy and bed plate preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Get measurements correct when spacing out parts; example bed plate for 15" model: brass sheet 1/16" thick, cut 4 × 14 inches, with accurately placed square hole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center holes and components carefully—mistakes will cause lopsided or non-working models. File and dress bed plate smooth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wheel construction and matching diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn wheel tires to the correct form and ensure driving wheels are exactly the same diameter so both travel equally per revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rim should project a little over 1/16" and edges beveled correctly. Spokes filed smooth; drill axle center before removing from lathe. Solder or wedge axles to wheels securely. Mismatched wheel diameters cause the engine to travel in circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crankshaft and crank throw relation to cylinder stroke
rubrics_metrics.description: Cranks should be at right angles and throw should be half the distance of the cylinder stroke (e.g., 1.5" stroke → 3/4" throw).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ease crank size to prevent piston knocking cylinder ends. Hammer and heat crankshaft while shaping; ensure correct geometry for smooth running.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiler construction and leak prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the boiler with care—use copper tubing, rivet if possible, turn brass ends, solder neatly, and ensure all joints and tubes are steam-tight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn ends and solder with care, hammer down projecting flanges, use old worn file when filing soldered joints, and re-solder any pin-sized holes—very small holes can prevent achieving steam pressure. Use tubes threaded and sealed with white lead and nuts to avoid leakage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smokestack, tube, and steam chest fitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Drill and fit smokestack, solder and position inside tube-box, fit steam chest, position steam pipe and safety valve with appropriate mountings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure box top is not more than half way up boiler; solder from outside to protect lamp flame; fit steam pipe so top is ~1/4" from inside top of steam chest. Make and fit safety valve, spring case, manhole screwhead with leather washer for steam-tight refill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lamp and fuel for model operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a small lamp (tin box with brass tubes for wicks) to burn methylated alcohol; use for heating the model boiler to produce steam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wick and fuel placement: fill ~3/4 full with methylated alcohol; insert wicks in brass tubes; ensure taps closed before lighting. Lamp plus tender design allow model to run without rails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tender and vehicle weight considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Make tender as light as possible (tin is best) because each car added reduces engine speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wheels and axles for tender finished like engine; tender can serve as alcohol tank with soldered tin lining and fill screw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan and scale for large models
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide desired size, sketch the model full-size, and scale measurements proportionately; recognize larger models require costlier castings and materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 20 example: dimensions and scale (1/8" scale shown). Accurate full-size plans simplify measurement and reduce errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large model framework and measurement practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut frame-work from 1/8" sheet iron, keep parts central on reference line, and measure from a given center to ensure accuracy; slots and decorative holes specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow provided dimensions for slots and centers (examples given). Rivet or fasten frames to bed plate as described; ornament holes can be omitted as they are not structural.
